anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Transverse waves > Worked Example 1: Applying the two-arrow test for transverse waves: "Plucking a guitar string displaces the string segments at right angles to the wave speed."
title: Classifying Wave Types Using Oscillation Direction
action: Select the row that correctly classifies both seismic P-waves and visible light waves, stating the correct oscillation direction relative to energy propagation.
prompt: Which row correctly identifies the wave classification and the direction of particle oscillation relative to energy propagation for seismic P-waves and for visible light?

options.text: Seismic P-waves: longitudinal (oscillations parallel to energy propagation); Visible light: transverse (oscillations perpendicular to energy propagation)
Seismic P-waves: transverse (oscillations perpendicular to energy propagation); Visible light: longitudinal (oscillations parallel to energy propagation)
Seismic P-waves: longitudinal (oscillations perpendicular to energy propagation); Visible light: transverse (oscillations parallel to energy propagation)
Seismic P-waves: transverse (oscillations parallel to energy propagation); Visible light: transverse (oscillations perpendicular to energy propagation)

feedback.A: Correct. Seismic P-waves are longitudinal compressional waves where rock particles oscillate parallel to energy propagation. Visible light is an electromagnetic wave where oscillating fields are perpendicular to energy propagation.
feedback.B: Incorrect. P-waves are longitudinal, not transverse. Visible light is transverse, not longitudinal.
feedback.C: Incorrect. In longitudinal waves, oscillations are parallel (not perpendicular) to energy propagation. In transverse waves, oscillations are perpendicular (not parallel).
feedback.D: Incorrect. P-waves are longitudinal waves, not transverse waves. Furthermore, transverse waves have perpendicular, not parallel, oscillations.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Compressions and rarefactions: "The shortest distance between a compression and an adjacent rarefaction equals half of a wavelength."
title: Longitudinal Wave Spacing and Wavelength
action: Select the correct statement relating the spatial separation of compressions and rarefactions to the wavelength lambda of a longitudinal wave.
prompt: In a progressive longitudinal sound wave travelling through air, what is the shortest distance between the centre of a compression and the centre of an adjacent rarefaction?

options.text: lambda / 2, because a compression and an adjacent rarefaction are in antiphase.
lambda, because one wavelength is the distance between any two distinct features in the wave.
lambda / 4, because a compression is a quarter-cycle ahead of a rarefaction.
2 lambda, because two regions of different density are required to form a full cycle.

feedback.A: Correct. A compression (maximum density) and an adjacent rarefaction (minimum density) represent opposite phases (antiphase) of the wave cycle. Their separation is half of a wavelength, lambda / 2.
feedback.B: Incorrect. One full wavelength lambda is the distance between consecutive points in identical phase, such as from one compression to the next compression.
feedback.C: Incorrect. A compression and the adjacent rarefaction are separated by a phase difference of 180 degrees (pi radians), which corresponds to half a wavelength (lambda / 2), not a quarter wavelength.
feedback.D: Incorrect. Two consecutive compressions span one wavelength lambda, so the distance to the intermediate rarefaction is lambda / 2, not 2 lambda.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Graphical representations of waves: "A displacement-time graph records the oscillation history of one single particle at a fixed position."
title: Interpreting Wave Graphs by Axis Inspection
action: Select the option that correctly identifies the physical quantity obtained from the horizontal peak-to-peak separation in a displacement-distance graph and a displacement-time graph.
prompt: A student inspects two sinusoidal wave graphs. Graph X plots displacement against distance, and Graph Y plots displacement against time. Which row correctly identifies what the peak-to-peak horizontal separation represents on each graph?

options.text: Graph X: wavelength lambda; Graph Y: period T
Graph X: period T; Graph Y: wavelength lambda
Graph X: wave speed v; Graph Y: frequency f
Graph X: wavelength lambda; Graph Y: wave speed v

feedback.A: Correct. A displacement-distance graph is a spatial snapshot where horizontal separation gives wavelength lambda. A displacement-time graph shows the temporal history of one point where horizontal separation gives period T.
feedback.B: Incorrect. This reverses the roles of the axes. Distance cannot give period in seconds, and time cannot give wavelength in metres.
feedback.C: Incorrect. Wave speed cannot be read directly from a peak-to-peak separation on either graph; it must be calculated using v = f lambda or v = lambda / T.
feedback.D: Incorrect. While Graph X gives wavelength lambda, Graph Y gives period T, not wave speed.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Instantaneous particle motion on a travelling wave: "At a positive displacement crest, the particle reaches its turning point and has zero instantaneous velocity."
title: Determining Instantaneous Particle Velocity on a Travelling Wave
action: Select the option that correctly states the instantaneous direction of motion for a particle at an equilibrium zero-crossing on a rising slope of a rightward-travelling transverse wave.
prompt: A transverse wave travels from left to right along a horizontal rope. At time t0, point P is at zero displacement on an upward-sloping section of the wave profile. What is the instantaneous direction of motion of the rope particle at point P?

options.text: Vertically downwards, because shifting the wave profile slightly to the right places a negative displacement at point P.
Vertically upwards, because point P is located on an upward-sloping section of the wave.
Horizontally to the right, because the wave energy travels to the right.
Momentarily stationary, because point P is at the equilibrium position.

feedback.A: Correct. Applying the wave profile shift technique: as the wave profile shifts rightwards, the trough behind point P arrives at position P, so the particle must move vertically downwards.
feedback.B: Incorrect. This is a common misconception. On a rightward-travelling wave, an upward slope moves downward as the profile shifts forward.
feedback.C: Incorrect. Rope particles in a transverse wave oscillate perpendicular to energy propagation (vertically), never along the direction of wave travel.
feedback.D: Incorrect. Particles passing through equilibrium have maximum speed, not zero speed. Zero instantaneous velocity occurs at crests and troughs.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Longitudinal wave graphs and particle crowding: "At a downward zero-crossing, particles converge from both sides into a high-density compression."
title: Connecting Longitudinal Displacement Graphs to Medium Density
action: Select the statement that correctly identifies the physical condition of a medium at a downward zero-crossing on a longitudinal displacement-distance graph where positive displacement is defined as rightward.
prompt: A longitudinal wave travels to the right. On its displacement-distance graph, displacement to the right is plotted as positive. At position X, the displacement is zero and the graph has a negative gradient (downward-sloping zero-crossing). What physical condition occurs at position X?

options.text: A compression, because particles to the left are displaced rightwards and particles to the right are displaced leftwards toward position X.
A rarefaction, because particles to the left and right are displaced away from position X.
Normal equilibrium density, because the particle displacement at position X is zero.
A rarefaction, because a downward slope indicates decreasing medium pressure.

feedback.A: Correct. With positive displacement defined as rightwards, particles to the left of X have positive displacement (shifted right toward X) and particles to the right of X have negative displacement (shifted left toward X). Particles converge at X, creating a compression with maximum density.
feedback.B: Incorrect. Divergence of particles occurs at an upward-sloping zero-crossing (positive gradient), which creates a rarefaction, not at a downward zero-crossing.
feedback.C: Incorrect. Zero displacement does not mean zero density change. At a downward zero-crossing, particles converge from both sides, producing maximum particle crowding and pressure.
feedback.D: Incorrect. The slope of the displacement graph represents the displacement gradient. A negative slope means converging displacements, which results in higher pressure (compression), not lower pressure.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Polarisation as a diagnostic test: "Because sound waves are longitudinal, their oscillations cannot be restricted to a single transverse plane."
title: Evaluating Wave Properties and Polarisation Capability
action: Select the option that correctly explains why sound waves cannot be polarised while light waves can be polarised.
prompt: Why can light waves undergo polarisation, whereas sound waves in air cannot undergo polarisation?

options.text: Light waves are transverse so their oscillations occur in planes perpendicular to travel, whereas sound waves are longitudinal so their oscillations are restricted to the direction of travel.
Sound waves have much longer wavelengths than light waves, making their oscillations too large to fit through polarising filters.
Light waves can travel through a vacuum, whereas sound waves require a material medium to transfer energy.
Sound waves are transverse in liquids and longitudinal in gases, so they cancel out any polarised oscillations.

feedback.A: Correct. Polarisation restricts oscillations to a single plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation. This is only possible for transverse waves (such as light). Longitudinal waves (such as sound) have oscillations already parallel to energy travel, so they cannot be polarised.
feedback.B: Incorrect. Polarisation is governed by the vector direction of oscillation relative to energy travel, not by wavelength size. Longitudinal waves of any wavelength cannot be polarised.
feedback.C: Incorrect. While light travels through vacuum and sound requires a medium, this does not explain polarisation capability. Transverse waves in solids (like seismic S-waves) can also be polarised.
feedback.D: Incorrect. Sound waves are longitudinal in gases, liquids, and solids alike; fluids cannot support transverse sound waves.
